results.title: Generalized torsion element (Kourovka 16.49)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An element $h$ of a group $H$ is a generalized torsion element when $h \ne 1$ and some nonempty product of conjugates of $h$ is trivial, that is, $x_1^{-1} h x_1 \cdots x_k^{-1} h x_k = 1$ for some $k \ge 1$ and some $x_1, \dots, x_k \in H$.

results.title: Free products of groups without generalized torsion have no generalized torsion
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Generalized torsion elements (Kourovka 16.48)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An element $h$ of a group $H$ is a generalized torsion element if $h \ne 1$ and there are $n \ge 1$ elements $x_1, \dots, x_n \in H$, not necessarily distinct, such that $(x_1^{-1} h x_1)(x_2^{-1} h x_2) \cdots (x_n^{-1} h x_n) = 1$.

results.title: Right orders on a group (Kourovka 16.48)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The right orders of a group $G$ are the binary relations $\preceq$ on $G$ that are linear orders (reflexive, transitive, antisymmetric and total) and are invariant under right multiplication: $a \preceq b$ implies $ac \preceq bc$ for all $a, b, c \in G$.

results.title: The Kopytov–Medvedev question (Kourovka 16.48)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: This is the proposition that every group $H$ with no generalized torsion element is right-orderable, that is, admits a right order.

results.title: Some group without generalized torsion is not right-orderable (Kourovka 16.48)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Kopytov–Medvedev proposition is false: there is a group $H$ with no generalized torsion element that admits no right order.

results.title: Scaled monotonicity of binomial coefficients
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For natural numbers $r$, $M$ and $N$ with $r \le M \le N$, we have $N^r \binom{M}{r} \le M^r \binom{N}{r}$.

results.title: Erdős layer criterion, factorial form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $N$ and $r$ be natural numbers with $0 < N$, $r \le N$, $2r \le N$ and $6 \le N$. For a natural number $x$ write $x\#$ for the primorial of $x$, the product of all primes $p \le x$, and let $L = \lfloor \log_2 N \rfloor$. If $r! \cdot \lfloor N/3 \rfloor\# \cdot \prod_{m=2}^{L} \lfloor N^{1/m} \rfloor\# < (N + 1 - r)^r$, then the binomial coefficient $\binom{N}{r}$ has a prime factor $p > r$.

results.title: Erdős layer criterion, power-of-four form

If $r \cdot \lfloor N/3 \rfloor\# \cdot \prod_{m=2}^{L} \lfloor N^{1/m} \rfloor\# < 4^r$, then the binomial coefficient $\binom{N}{r}$ has a prime factor $p > r$.

results.title: Maximum region count for three-armed V's
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A long-legged three-armed V is the union of three rays $\{c + s u_j : s \ge 0\}$, $j = 1, 2, 3$, from a common tip $c \in \mathbb{R}^2$, with nonzero direction vectors $u_1, u_2, u_3 \in \mathbb{R}^2$ in arbitrary directions. results.title: Weakly convergent sequences are norm-bounded
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $(u_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $E$ and let $x \in E$. If $f(u_n) \to f(x)$ as $n \to \infty$ for every continuous linear functional $f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$, then the norms are bounded above: there is a real number $C$ with $\|u_n\| \le C$ for all $n$.

results.title: Weak lower semicontinuity of the norm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $(u_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $E$ and let $x \in E$. If $f(u_n) \to f(x)$ as $n \to \infty$ for every continuous linear functional $f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$, that is, $u_n$ converges weakly to $x$, then $\|x\| \le \liminf_{n \to \infty} \|u_n\|$.

results.title: Bounded operators preserve weak convergence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ and $F$ be normed spaces over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, let $T \colon E \to F$ be a continuous linear map, let $(u_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $E$ and let $x \in E$. If $f(u_n) \to f(x)$ for every continuous linear functional $f \colon E \to \mathbb{K}$, then $g(T u_n) \to g(T x)$ for every continuous linear functional $g \colon F \to \mathbb{K}$.

results.title: Root-valid B-trees are valid
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a tree satisfies the root invariant for minimum degree $t$ at height $h$, then for some natural number $m$ it satisfies the structural invariant for minimum degree $t$, minimum top-node key count $m$ and height $h$.

results.title: B-tree search
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a linearly ordered key type, the search for a key $x$ in a raw B-tree proceeds as follows. At a leaf, report whether $x$ is in the leaf's key list. At an internal node with separators $k_1, \dots, k_m$ and children $c_0, c_1, \dots$, scan the separators in order. On reaching $k_i$, report failure if the node has no child $c_{i-1}$; otherwise search $c_{i-1}$ if $x < k_i$, report success if $x = k_i$, and move…

results.title: Result of inserting into a B-tree subtree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An insertion result over a key type $\alpha$ is either a single tree over $\alpha$, or a triple $(\ell, m, r)$ of two trees $\ell$ and $r$ over $\alpha$ and a key $m$ of $\alpha$. In insertion, the first form is a subtree that did not split, and the second form is an overflowing node split into two trees of the same height, with the median key $m$ promoted between them; the type itself does not record heights.

results.title: Flattening of a B-tree insertion result
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The flattening of an insertion result that is a single tree is the flattening of that tree; for a result that splits into a left tree $\ell$, a promoted median key $m$ and a right tree $r$, it is the flattening of $\ell$, followed by $m$, followed by the flattening of $r$.

results.title: Insertion into a B-tree leaf
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Over a linearly ordered key type, let $t$ be a natural number, $x$ a key, $K$ the key list of a leaf, and $K'$ the result of ordered insertion of $x$ into $K$. If $K'$ has at most $2t - 1$ keys, the insertion result is the single leaf with keys $K'$. Otherwise the leaf is split: the result consists of the leaf holding the first $t - 1$ keys of $K'$, the next key of $K'$ promoted as the median, and the leaf holding…

results.title: Splitting a B-tree node
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $t$ be a minimum degree, $s = t - 1$ (so $s = 0$ when $t = 0$), $k_1, \dots, k_m$ a list of keys and $c_1, \dots, c_n$ a list of B-trees. If $m > s$, splitting returns the pair of internal nodes formed by the keys $k_1, \dots, k_s$ with the first $t$ children (all of them if $n < t$) and by the keys $k_{s+2}, \dots, k_m$ with the children after the first $t$, together with the key $k_{s+1}$ promoted between…

results.title: Rebuilding an internal node after insertion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For minimum degree $t$, a separator list $K$ and a child list $C$, the result is the internal node with separators $K$ and children $C$, kept as a single tree when $K$ has at most $2t - 1$ keys, and otherwise split by node splitting into two nodes and a promoted median key.

results.title: Split-returning insertion into a B-tree subtree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For minimum degree $t$ and a key $x$, insertion of $x$ into a tree returns an insertion result and is defined by recursion. At a leaf with key list $K$, it is leaf insertion of $x$ into $K$. At an internal node, the separator list and the child list are scanned together from the left. If $x$ is smaller than the current separator, or no separator is left but a child is, $x$ is inserted into the current child. If $x$…

results.title: B-tree insertion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For minimum degree $t$, the tree obtained by inserting a key $x$ into a tree $T$ is computed from the split-returning insertion of $x$ into $T$: if that returns a single tree, this tree is the result; if it returns two trees $\ell$ and $r$ with a promoted median key $m$, the result is a new root node with the single separator $m$ and the two children $\ell$ and $r$.

results.title: The empty B-tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The empty B-tree is the leaf with no keys.

results.title: B-trees of a given minimum degree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A tree $T$ is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ when $t \ge 2$ (the CLRS Chapter 18 minimum-degree requirement), $T$ is ordered, and $T$ is root-valid at some height. This is the invariant preserved by insertion and by building a tree from a list.

results.title: The minimum degree of a B-tree is at least two
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a tree is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$, then $t \ge 2$.

results.title: B-trees are ordered
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a tree is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$, then it is ordered: each key of its inorder flattening is less than every key that comes after it.

results.title: B-trees satisfy the root invariant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $T$ is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$, then there is a height $h$ such that $T$ satisfies the root structural invariant of minimum degree $t$ at height $h$.

results.title: The empty tree is a B-tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every key type equipped with a binary relation $<$ and every natural number $t \ge 2$, the empty B-tree is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$.

results.title: B-tree insertion as sorted list insertion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be linearly ordered, let $t \ge 2$, and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$. For every key $x \in \alpha$, the inorder flattening of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ with minimum degree $t$ equals the sorted insertion of $x$ into the inorder flattening of $T$.

results.title: Membership after B-tree insertion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For all keys $x$ and $y$, $y$ belongs to the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ belongs to $T$.

results.title: Insertion preserves the B-tree invariant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let the keys come from a linearly ordered type. If $T$ is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$, then for every key $x$ the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ is again a B-tree of minimum degree $t$: it is ordered and root-valid at some height.

results.title: Correctness of B-tree search
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be linearly ordered and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$. For every key $x \in \alpha$, the search procedure returns true on $x$ and $T$ if and only if $x$ is a member of $T$, that is, $x$ occurs in the inorder flattening of $T$.

results.title: Size of a B-tree after insertion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be linearly ordered, let $t \ge 2$, let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, and let $x \in \alpha$. Let $T'$ be the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $T$ with minimum degree $t$. If $x$ occurs in the inorder flattening of $T$, then the flattening of $T'$ has the same length as that of $T$; otherwise it is one longer.

results.title: B-tree built from a list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a linearly ordered key type and a natural number $t$, the tree built from the empty list is the empty tree, and the tree built from a list with head $x$ and tail $L$ is the result of inserting $x$, with minimum degree $t$, into the tree built from $L$. Thus the elements are inserted from right to left.

results.title: Building from a list yields a B-tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a linearly ordered key type, every natural number $t \ge 2$ and every list $L$ of keys, the tree obtained by inserting the elements of $L$ from right to left into the empty tree, each insertion with minimum degree $t$, is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$.

results.title: Membership in a B-tree built from a list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $xs$ be a list over a linearly ordered key type. A key $x$ belongs to the tree of minimum degree $t$ built from $xs$ (by inserting the elements of $xs$ into the empty tree, from right to left) if and only if $x$ is an element of $xs$.

results.title: Building a B-tree from a strictly increasing list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$. For every strictly increasing list $L$ of keys, the tree built from $L$ by inserting its keys from right to left into the empty tree with minimum degree $t$ has flattening exactly $L$.

results.title: B-tree deletion by rebuilding
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a minimum degree $t$, a key $x$ and a tree $T$, the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ is the tree obtained by inserting the keys of the list $L$, from right to left, into the empty tree with B-tree insertion of minimum degree $t$, where $L$ is the inorder flattening of $T$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed ($L$ is the flattening itself when $x$ does not occur in it).

results.title: Rebuilding deletion unfolds to erase and rebuild
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every minimum degree $t$, key $x$ and tree $T$, the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ equals the tree built from the list obtained by removing the first occurrence of $x$ from the flattening of $T$, by inserting its keys from right to left into the empty tree with minimum degree $t$.

results.title: Flattening after rebuilding deletion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$, let $T$ be an ordered tree and let $x$ be a key. The flattening of the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ is the flattening of $T$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed (unchanged if $x$ does not occur).

results.title: Rebuilding deletion yields a B-tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$. For every key $x$ and every tree $T$, whether or not $T$ is itself a B-tree, the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ is a B-tree of minimum degree $t$.

results.title: Rebuild deletion yields an ordered tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let keys come from a linearly ordered type. For every key $x$ and every tree $T$, not necessarily ordered, the tree obtained from $T$ by rebuild deletion of $x$ (removing the first occurrence of $x$, if any, from the inorder flattening of $T$ and rebuilding a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ from the remaining keys) is ordered: its inorder flattening is strictly increasing.

results.title: Rebuilding deletion yields a root-valid tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$. For every key $x$ and every tree $T$, there is a height $h$ such that the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ is root-valid of minimum degree $t$ and height $h$: all leaves sit at depth $h$, every node holds at most $2t - 1$ keys, every non-root node holds at least $t - 1$ keys, an internal root holds at least one key, and an internal node with $k$ keys has $k + 1$ children.

results.title: Membership after rebuild deletion from a B-tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type. For all keys $x$ and $y$, the key $y$ lies in the tree obtained from $T$ by rebuild deletion of $x$ (erasing $x$ from the inorder flattening of $T$ and rebuilding a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ from the remaining keys) if and only if $y \ne x$ and $y$ lies in $T$.

results.title: The deleted key is absent after rebuild deletion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ with keys in a linearly ordered type. For every key $x$, the tree obtained from $T$ by rebuild deletion of $x$ (erasing $x$ from the inorder flattening of $T$ and rebuilding a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ from the remaining keys) does not contain $x$.

results.title: Search after rebuilding deletion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$, let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$, and let $x$ and $y$ be keys. The B-tree search for $y$ in the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ returns true if and only if $y \ne x$ and $y$ is stored in $T$.

results.title: Rebuilding deletion of an absent key
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$, let $T$ be an ordered tree and let $x$ be a key that does not occur in the flattening of $T$. Then the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ has the same flattening as $T$.

results.title: Key count after rebuilding deletion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$, let $T$ be an ordered tree with flattening of length $n$, and let $x$ be a key. The flattening of the rebuilding deletion of $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ has length $n - 1$ if $x$ occurs in the flattening of $T$, and length $n$ otherwise.

results.title: Rebuilding deletion of the same key twice
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$, let $T$ be an ordered tree (its flattening is strictly increasing) and let $x$ be a key. Deleting $x$ twice by rebuilding with minimum degree $t$ gives a tree with the same flattening as deleting $x$ once.

results.title: Number of keys at the root of a B-tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a raw B-tree $T$, this is the length of the key list stored at the root of $T$: the number of keys of $T$ if $T$ is a leaf, and the number of separator keys of $T$ if $T$ is an internal node. Keys in the children are not counted.

results.title: Splitting off the last element of a list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a nonempty list $l$, the result is the pair consisting of $l$ with its last element removed and the last element of $l$; for the empty list there is no result.

results.title: Rightmost key of a B-tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a tree $T$, the rightmost key of $T$ is an optional key defined by descending the rightmost spine: for a leaf it is the last of its keys (none if the leaf has no keys); for an internal node with at least one child it is the rightmost key of its last child; for an internal node with no children it is the last of its separator keys (none if there are none).

results.title: Leftmost key of a B-tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a tree $T$, the leftmost key of $T$ is an optional key defined by descending the leftmost spine: for a leaf it is the first of its keys (none if the leaf has no keys); for an internal node with at least one child it is the leftmost key of its first child; for an internal node with no children it is the first of its separator keys (none if there are none).

results.title: Merging two B-tree nodes around a separator
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a key $s$ and trees $L$ and $R$, the merge of $L$ and $R$ around $s$ is defined as follows. If $L$ and $R$ are leaves with key lists $k_1$ and $k_2$, it is the leaf with keys $k_1$, then $s$, then $k_2$. If $L$ and $R$ are internal nodes with key lists $k_1, k_2$ and child lists $c_1, c_2$, it is the internal node with keys $k_1$, then $s$, then $k_2$, and children $c_1$ followed by $c_2$. In every other case…

results.title: Borrowing a key from the right sibling
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a tree $c$ (the child), a separator key $k$ and a tree $s$ (the right sibling) such that $c$ and $s$ are both leaves or both internal nodes, $s$ has at least one key, and, when they are internal nodes, $s$ has at least one child: $k$ becomes the last key of $c$, the first key of $s$ is removed from $s$ and becomes the new separator, and, for internal nodes, the first child of $s$ is removed from $s$ and…

results.title: Borrowing a key from the left sibling
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a tree $s$ (the left sibling), a separator key $k$ and a tree $c$ (the child) such that $s$ and $c$ are both leaves or both internal nodes, $s$ has at least one key, and, when they are internal nodes, $s$ has at least one child: the last key of $s$ is removed from $s$ and becomes the new separator, $k$ becomes the first key of $c$, and, for internal nodes, the last child of $s$ is removed from $s$ and becomes…

results.title: Deletion within a B-tree node
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $D$ be an operation that deletes a key from a tree, let $t$ be a natural number, let $x$ be a key of a linearly ordered key type, and write $|c|$ for the number of keys stored at the root of a tree $c$. Deleting $x$ within a node with separator list $K$ and child list $C$, using $D$ on children, produces a new separator list and a new child list. Write $k$ for the first separator, $c$ for the first child, and…

results.title: Height-indexed B-tree deletion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a height $h$, a minimum degree $t$, a key $x$ of a linearly ordered key type and a tree $T$, the result is defined as follows. If $T$ is a leaf, the result is the leaf whose key list is that of $T$ with the first occurrence of $x$ erased, whatever $h$ is. If $T$ is an internal node and $h = 0$, the result is $T$. If $T$ is an internal node and $h = n + 1$, the result is the internal node whose separator and…

results.title: Height of a B-tree along first children
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The height of a B-tree is computed by following first children: a leaf has height $0$, an internal node with no children has height $0$, and an internal node whose first child is $c$ has height one more than the height of $c$.

results.title: Top-down B-tree deletion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Deleting a key $x$ of a linearly ordered key type from a tree $T$ with minimum degree $t$ applies height-indexed deletion of $x$ with minimum degree $t$ to $T$ at the height of $T$, where the height of a leaf, or of an internal node without children, is $0$, and the height of any other internal node is one more than the height of its first child. If the outcome is an internal node with no keys and exactly one…

results.title: Deletion from a B-tree erases the key from its flattening
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For every key $x$, the inorder flattening of the tree obtained from $T$ by top-down deletion of $x$ with minimum degree $t$ is the flattening of $T$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed (unchanged if $x$ does not occur).

results.title: Top-down deletion lowers the height by at most one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be an ordered tree over a linearly ordered key type (its inorder flattening is strictly increasing) that satisfies the root invariant of B-trees of minimum degree $t$ at height $h$. For every key $x$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ satisfies the root invariant of minimum degree $t$ at height $h$ or at height $h - 1$, where $h - 1$ is truncated…

results.title: Top-down deletion preserves the B-tree invariant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For every key $x$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ is again a B-tree of minimum degree $t$.

results.title: Deletion from a B-tree yields an ordered tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For every key $x$, the tree obtained from $T$ by deleting $x$ (with minimum degree $t$) is ordered: its inorder flattening is strictly increasing.

results.title: Top-down deletion yields a root-valid tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For every key $x$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ satisfies the root invariant of B-trees of minimum degree $t$ at some height.

results.title: Membership after deletion from a B-tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For all keys $x$ and $y$, $y$ belongs to the tree obtained from $T$ by deleting $x$ (with minimum degree $t$) if and only if $y \ne x$ and $y$ belongs to $T$.

results.title: The deleted key is absent after deletion from a B-tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For every key $x$, $x$ does not belong to the tree obtained from $T$ by deleting $x$ (with minimum degree $t$).

results.title: Search after top-down deletion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For all keys $x$ and $y$, searching for $y$ in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $T$ with minimum degree $t$ succeeds if and only if $y \ne x$ and $y$ is a key of $T$.

results.title: Deletion shortens the flattening by one exactly when the key is present
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$, let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type, and let $x$ be a key. If $x$ occurs in the inorder flattening of $T$, the flattening of the tree obtained from $T$ by deleting $x$ (with minimum degree $t$) has length one less than the flattening of $T$; otherwise the two flattenings have the same length.

results.title: Repeated top-down deletion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t \ge 2$ and let $T$ be a B-tree of minimum degree $t$ over a linearly ordered key type. For every key $x$, deleting $x$ from $T$ twice with minimum degree $t$ gives a tree with the same inorder flattening as deleting $x$ from $T$ once.

results.title: Simultaneous minimum and maximum
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a list $xs$ over a linearly ordered type, the paired algorithm returns no result when $xs$ is empty and otherwise returns a pair (a candidate minimum and a candidate maximum), counting one unit of time for each comparison of elements. On a one-element list $[a]$ it returns $(a, a)$ without a comparison. On a longer list of odd length both candidates start at the first element without a comparison; on a list…

results.title: Correctness of the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $xs$ over a linearly ordered type, the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm returns no result on $xs$ when $xs$ is empty, and returns the pair $(\min xs, \max xs)$ of the least and greatest elements of $xs$ otherwise.

results.title: The min–max algorithm returns no result exactly on the empty list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $xs$ over a linearly ordered type, the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm returns no result on $xs$ if and only if $xs$ is empty.

results.title: Characterization of the min–max output
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $xs$ over a linearly ordered type and all elements $lo$ and $hi$ of that type, the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm returns the pair $(lo, hi)$ on $xs$ if and only if $lo$ and $hi$ both belong to $xs$, $lo \le x$ for every $x$ in $xs$, and $x \le hi$ for every $x$ in $xs$.

results.title: The min–max algorithm on the empty list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: On the empty list, the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm returns no result and makes no comparisons.

results.title: The min–max algorithm on a one-element list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every element $a$ of a linearly ordered type, on the list $[a]$ the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm returns the pair $(a, a)$ and makes no comparisons.

results.title: Comparisons of the min–max algorithm on odd-length lists
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $k$ and every list of length $2k + 1$ over a linearly ordered type, the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm makes exactly $3k$ comparisons.

results.title: Comparisons of the min–max algorithm on even-length lists
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $k \ge 1$ and every list of length $2k$ over a linearly ordered type, the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm makes exactly $3k - 2$ comparisons.

results.title: Comparison count of the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list of length $n$ over a linearly ordered type, the simultaneous minimum and maximum algorithm makes no comparisons when $n = 0$ and exactly $\lceil 3n/2 \rceil - 2$ comparisons when $n \ge 1$.
